narrative:
The model predicted an 82% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your LSAT score, your class ranking after the third year of law school, and your undergraduate GPA. Your LSAT score was by far the strongest driver, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Scoring 24 compared with an average of 37 among accepted students created a large gap that the model interpreted as a significant obstacle to passing the bar. Your third-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; you placed in the second decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile, indicating your grades were substantially below the typical successful applicant. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.60, while below the accepted average of 3.23, actually worked slightly in your favor relative to the other factors, but not enough to offset the stronger negative signals.

Taken together, these academic performance indicators led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. You should focus on improving your LSAT score through targeted preparation, consider retaking courses or seeking additional academic support to raise future grades, and then reapply once you can demonstrate stronger performance in these key areas.
